ai.definition: Green Hydrogen is produced by electrolysis using renewable electricity to split water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen, emitting only water as a byproduct.
ai.howItWorks: Electrolysers apply an electric current from renewable sources (such as wind or solar) through water, splitting it into hydrogen and oxygen via the electrolysis process. The reaction is: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. The produced hydrogen can be stored and used for various applications including fuel cells in vehicles or industrial processes.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the need for clean energy solutions, particularly for sectors that are difficult to electrify such as heavy industry, long-haul transportation (shipping and aviation), and certain chemical manufacturing processes.
ai.manufacturing: The production of green hydrogen involves large-scale electrolyser plants which can be standalone or integrated into existing renewable energy infrastructure. The components include electrodes, membranes, and the overall system design for efficiency and durability.
ai.buildProcess: Construction begins with site selection, followed by detailed engineering, procurement, construction (EPC) phase, and commissioning. Key factors in the build process are the availability of renewable energy sources, water supply, and local regulations regarding emissions and safety standards.
ai.costDrivers: Costs are driven primarily by the capital expenditure for electrolyser equipment, operational costs related to electricity prices, maintenance, and potential subsidies or incentives from governments aimed at promoting green hydrogen adoption.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive with increasing government support and investment in renewable energy projects. However, significant scaling up of production capacities and cost reductions are needed to make it competitive with traditional fuels on a large scale.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary widely but generally focus on promoting the use of green hydrogen through incentives, setting emission standards, and mandating the decarbonization of certain industries. International cooperation is also driving standardization efforts for green hydrogen technologies.
ai.risks: Technical risks include efficiency losses in electrolysis processes, material degradation over time, and potential safety issues with high-pressure storage tanks. Economic risks stem from fluctuating renewable energy prices and competition from other low-carbon fuels like biofuels or synthetic fuels.
ai.profitability: Current profitability is limited due to higher costs compared to conventional hydrogen production methods. However, as technology improves and economies of scale are achieved, the potential for profitability increases significantly.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving electrolyser efficiency, reducing capital costs, and integrating more advanced renewable energy sources like offshore wind or concentrated solar power (CSP).

glossary.def: The process of using an electric current to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction, typically the splitting of water into hydrogen and oxygen.
Energy derived from natural resources that are replenished at a higher rate than they are consumed, such as solar, wind, or hydroelectric power.
Hydrogen produced through the electrolysis of water using renewable energy sources to ensure zero carbon emissions during production.

subsystems.name: Electrolyser stacks
subsystems.role: split water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity.
parts: electrodes and catalysts (nickel for alkaline; platinum and iridium for PEM)

subsystems.name: Renewable power supply
subsystems.role: the source that makes it 'green' — and the largest share of the cost.
parts: grid connection or power purchase agreement

subsystems.name: Compression and storage
subsystems.role: hydrogen is very light, so it must be compressed or converted to store.

subsystems.name: Delivery and offtake
subsystems.role: gets hydrogen to users or converts it.

buildSteps.title: Secure clean power
buildSteps.detail: Build or contract wind and solar supply; cheap, plentiful electricity decides whether the project is viable.

buildSteps.title: Manufacture stacks
buildSteps.detail: Catalysts are coated onto electrodes, and membranes, electrodes and plates are assembled into stacks of many cells.

buildSteps.title: Treat the water
buildSteps.detail: Feed water is desalinated and demineralised; impurities would foul the stack.

buildSteps.title: Integrate the plant
buildSteps.detail: Rectifiers feed DC to the stacks; separators, dryers and purifiers are plumbed in.

buildSteps.title: Operate
buildSteps.detail: Current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen; the hydrogen is purified and compressed.

buildSteps.title: Store and ship
buildSteps.detail: Hydrogen goes into tanks, caverns or pipelines, or is converted to ammonia or methanol, which are easier to ship.

prerequisites.why: the core machines are mature; the challenge is making them cheap at scale.
electricity is most of the cost of each kilogram of hydrogen.
iridium is so scarce it could cap PEM production.
few pipelines or large stores exist, so most projects must use hydrogen on site.
steel, ammonia and fuel makers must sign long contracts before plants get financed.

pathway.milestone: projects of tens to hundreds of megawatts
pathway.unlocks: operating experience; most hydrogen is still made from natural gas.

pathway.milestone: gigawatt-scale plants at sunny, windy export hubs
pathway.unlocks: economies of scale in stacks and power supply.
the uses where hydrogen has no cheaper clean alternative.
wide adoption — which needs cheap power and plants that run most of the day.
